Mission-critical is a budget discipline, not a server label

Mission-critical is a contract: payments clear, trading windows hold, clinical systems respond — with availability and latency targets that carry regulatory or revenue consequences. The engineering is unromantic: latency budgets allocated per hop and measured in production, redundancy that fails over in drills, and capacity modeled against the worst credible day.

High-performance work — inference at scale, event processing at peaks, low-latency paths — rides the same discipline: profile first, budget every layer, and prove the tail with load that exceeds anything the business calendar will throw at it.
Below: the failure modes that make 'HA' paper, the reference architecture of budgeted tiers, and the console that reports the rolling numbers.
Four failure modes that make high availability paper
Every one of these survives a whiteboard and dies in a drill — the countermeasures put clocks on failover, budgets on latency and models on capacity.

widgets.title: Failure-domain map — click nodes for the independence contract

nodes.label: Multi-CDN edge
nodes.detail: Two CDNs with independent contracts and health checks; the DNS layer fails over on synthetic probes, not on human seeing a dashboard.

nodes.label: Region A active
nodes.detail: Full stack active; writes commit with quorum spanning regions — a zonal loss inside A is invisible to clients.

nodes.label: Region B active-standby
nodes.detail: Receives the replication stream with freshness verified by replay lag alarms; assumes load on drill schedule, not only on disaster.

nodes.label: Quorum storage
nodes.detail: Writes commit across regions with documented conflict semantics; the split-brain answer is decided in the design, not in the incident.

nodes.label: Independent secrets
nodes.detail: Each region holds its own secrets plane with break-glass material — a secrets outage in A cannot lock out B.

nodes.label: Control plane
nodes.detail: The audited shared-fate surface: deploy pipeline and global config. Its blast radius is measured and its changes are gated by the drill calendar.

widgets.note: Click nodes for the independence contract each domain carries. The control plane is honest about being shared fate — gated, measured, drilled.

widgets.title: Last drill cycle — recovery against signed targets
widgets.note: Gauges show drill evidence against signed targets with warn/crit bands. RPO effective is measured by replay verification, not assumed from replication marketing.

widgets.title: Capacity headroom what-if — burst shape vs degradation plan
widgets.note: The knee in the p99.9 curve is the autoscale ceiling — past it, latency degrades non-linearly and the shed plan earns its keep. Drag the ceiling against realistic peaks.

The tier spans network, data and clients; these contracts define what each layer must deliver for the end-to-end budget to hold under peak load.
Tail-governance overlay

The tail is governed as strictly as the average: p99 regressions gate releases, load models are re-signed quarterly, and capacity headroom is a reviewed number — because the users who leave live in the tail.

blocks.x: Failover drills run with production-like data volumes and the clock published internally: a drill that exceeds its time budget produces findings with owners, and the next drill re-tests them first.
Ask when your failover was last rehearsed with production-like volume. If the answer is 'never', bring the tier to a briefing — the first drill is complimentary, the outage is not.
